finding.claim: With caching enabled, a signed token that has `exp` but no numeric `iat` is cached with no expiry bound from `exp`. The cache entry lives for the full cacheTTL (default 10 minutes), so the cache keeps returning the payload as valid after the token has expired.
finding.source: A signed JWT with an `exp` claim and no numeric `iat`, presented to a verifier created with `cache` enabled. The attacker could be a holder of a legitimately issued token, or of a leaked one, that omits `iat`.
finding.sink: The cache-hit branch in verify() (src/verifier.js:362-378) returns the cached payload as a successful verification.

trace.note: hasIat is false when payload.iat is not a number
The block that reads nbf and exp is skipped, so cacheValue[1] and cacheValue[2] stay 0
cacheValue[2] === 0, so it is set to maxTTL = now + clockTolerance + cacheTTL, ignoring exp
On a later call, min === 0 and now <= max, so the lookup is treated as a hit
The cached payload is returned without re-checking exp, so no TokenError is thrown

finding.guards_checked: validateClaimDateValue runs only on a cache miss in verifyToken, so it does not cover this path. The cache-hit range check uses max, which is the cacheTTL cap for these tokens. Setting ignoreExpiration disables the exp check entirely, so it does not apply here. The default cacheTTL is 600000 ms. The finding needs a token with no iat, which is allowed unless requiredClaims includes iat. It only affects deployments that enable the cache.
